title: The Silent Evacuation of Gallipoli
text:
By late 1915 the Allied campaign on the Gallipoli peninsula had failed. Australian, New Zealand, British and other troops clung to narrow beachheads at Anzac Cove, Suvla Bay and Cape Helles, often only a few meters from the Ottoman trenches. When London decided to withdraw, some commanders feared that pulling out under the enemy's eyes could cost a large share of the force.

At Anzac the plan was largely drawn up by the Australian staff officer Brudenell White. Weeks beforehand, the troops held "silent" periods in which they stopped firing for long stretches, so the Turks grew used to quiet trenches. Then, over a series of nights in December, men were taken off in stages while those remaining kept up normal activity. Paths were marked, boots were muffled with sacking, and each man had a precise time and route to the beach.

The last groups left in the early hours of 20 December. To cover their departure, some rigged rifles to fire by themselves. The best known device, credited to Lance Corporal William Scurry, used water dripping from one tin into another until the weight pulled the trigger, so shots kept sounding from empty trenches after the men had gone.

Tens of thousands of men left Anzac and Suvla with almost no casualties, and Helles was evacuated just as cleanly in January 1916. It was the most successful operation of the entire campaign.
lesson: Careful planning, rehearsal and discipline across a whole team can turn a dangerous retreat into a success. Every person knowing their exact part is what keeps a plan silent.
people: Brudenell White, William Scurry, ANZAC and British forces
location: Anzac Cove, Suvla Bay and Cape Helles, Gallipoli peninsula, Turkey
source: C. E. W. Bean, The Official History of Australia in the War of 1914 to 1918, vol. 2 (1924)
